The integrand is radial, so use polar coordinates \((x,y)=(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\). For \(r>0\),

\[
dx\,dy=r\,dr\,d\theta,
\]

and

\[
r\cos(\pi r)+n^2r^3=r\bigl(\cos(\pi r)+n^2r^2\bigr).
\]

Thus, ignoring the measure-zero point \(r=0\),

\[
I_n
=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1
\frac{n}{r\cos(\pi r)+n^2r^3}\,r\,dr\,d\theta
=2\pi\int_0^1 \frac{n}{\cos(\pi r)+n^2r^2}\,dr.
\]

Now set \(t=nr\), so \(r=t/n\), \(dr=dt/n\). Then

\[
I_n
=2\pi\int_0^n \frac{dt}{\cos\left(\frac{\pi t}{n}\right)+t^2}.
\]

Define

\[
f_n(t)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{1}{\cos\left(\frac{\pi t}{n}\right)+t^2}, & 0\le t\le n,\\[1.2ex]
0, & t>n.
\end{cases}
\]

For each fixed \(t\ge 0\), as \(n\to\infty\),

\[
f_n(t)\to \frac{1}{1+t^2}.
\]

We can apply dominated convergence. For sufficiently large \(n\), on \(0\le t\le 2\),

\[
\cos\left(\frac{\pi t}{n}\right)\ge \cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{n}\right)>\frac12,
\]

so \(f_n(t)\le 2\). For \(t\ge 2\),

\[
\cos\left(\frac{\pi t}{n}\right)+t^2\ge t^2-1\ge \frac34t^2,
\]

so

\[
f_n(t)\le \frac{4}{3t^2}.
\]

Thus \(f_n\) is dominated by an integrable function on \([0,\infty)\). Therefore,

\[
